title: Forward Propagation in Action
description: Step through vectorized forward passes with matrix multiplication, layer-by-layer shape transformations, and batch processing.

slides.title: The Vectorized Forward Pass 📐
slides.content:
# Matrix Operations in Neural Networks

Modern hardware (GPUs and TPUs) computes forward passes using vectorized linear algebra. Instead of looping through individual neurons, we multiply entire matrices:

$$\mathbf{Z}_1 = \mathbf{X} \mathbf{W}_1 + \mathbf{b}_1$$
$$\mathbf{A}_1 = \text{ReLU}(\mathbf{Z}_1)$$
$$\mathbf{Z}_2 = \mathbf{A}_1 \mathbf{W}_2 + \mathbf{b}_2$$
$$\hat{\mathbf{Y}} = \sigma(\mathbf{Z}_2)$$

### Shape Transformations for Batch Size $N=64$:

| Layer Operation | Input Tensor Shape | Weight Matrix Shape | Bias Vector Shape | Output Tensor Shape |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Hidden Linear 1** | $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 10}$ | $\mathbf{W}_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{10 \times 32}$ | $\mathbf{b}_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times 32}$ | $\mathbf{Z}_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 32}$ |
| **Hidden Activation 1**| $\mathbf{Z}_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 32}$ | Element-wise ReLU | None | $\mathbf{A}_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 32}$ |
| **Output Linear 2** | $\mathbf{A}_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 32}$ | $\mathbf{W}_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{32 \times 2}$ | $\mathbf{b}_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times 2}$ | $\mathbf{Z}_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 2}$ |
| **Output Softmax** | $\mathbf{Z}_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 2}$ | Element-wise Softmax | None | $\hat{\mathbf{Y}} \in \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 2}$ |

quizData.question: If an input batch X has shape (32, 128) and the hidden layer has 64 neurons, what must be the dimension of the weight matrix W1?
quizData.explanation: Matrix multiplication requires inner dimensions to match: (32, 128) @ (128, 64) yields output batch shape (32, 64).

slides.title: Forward Pass from Scratch in NumPy 🐍
slides.content: A complete, vectorized 2-layer forward propagation implementation:
slides.codeSnippet:
import numpy as np

# Batch of 4 samples, 3 features
X = np.random.randn(4, 3)

# Layer 1: 3 in -> 5 hidden
W1 = np.random.randn(3, 5) * 0.1
b1 = np.zeros((1, 5))

# Layer 2: 5 hidden -> 1 output
W2 = np.random.randn(5, 1) * 0.1
b2 = np.zeros((1, 1))

# Forward propagation pass
Z1 = np.dot(X, W1) + b1
A1 = np.maximum(0, Z1) # ReLU
Z2 = np.dot(A1, W2) + b2
Y_hat = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-Z2)) # Sigmoid

print('Output probabilities shape:', Y_hat.shape)
print('Output batch probabilities:\n', Y_hat.round(3))

slides.title: AI Pro Tip: He / Xavier Weight Initialization 💡
slides.content:
## Never Initialize Weights to Zero
If you initialize all weights to zeros, every neuron in a layer computes the identical output and receives the identical backpropagation gradient. The neurons remain completely symmetric and never differentiate.

Always use random initialization scaled by fan-in/fan-out (He initialization for ReLU; Xavier/Glorot for Tanh/Sigmoid)!
